summary.text: A 73-year-old man with a long-term smoking history and no history of cardiovascular disease, diabetes or hypertension presented with sudden, persistent chest tightness for 3 days, orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. On examination he was orthopneic with widespread crackles, a Grade III–IV apical holosystolic murmur, blood pressure 90/74 mmHg, heart rate 103 beats per minute and 3+ bilateral leg edema.

The initial ECG upon admission showed poor R-wave progression (the Figure 1 caption also states ST segment depression); troponin I, myoglobin, CK-MB and NT-proBNP were measured, and HF following AMI was considered. Echocardiography showed anterolateral papillary muscle rupture with anterior leaflet prolapse and flail motion while LVEF was 60%, and chest CT showed pulmonary edema and pleural effusion. Recheck troponin and a second ECG showed pathological Q waves with persistent ST elevation; angiography, which could not be done in the emergency setting, showed LAD stenosis with thrombus, diagonal branch stenosis, obtuse marginal branch chronic total occlusion and RCA stenosis. The diagnosis was acute ST elevation myocardial infarction, Killip Class III–IV, complicated by papillary muscle rupture, severe mitral regurgitation and acute heart failure.

Preoperative treatment comprised noninvasive ventilation, antiplatelet, statin, diuretic and anticoagulant drugs, and morphine; after 17 days heart failure improved and he was weaned from ventilation, and NT-proBNP and Hs-CnTI fell. He underwent mechanical mitral valve replacement and coronary artery bypass grafting on the 18th day of admission, with postoperative pathology showing local ischemic necrosis. Low cardiac output syndrome, pulmonary infection and acute kidney injury followed and were treated with temporary pacing and dopamine. After 27 days of treatment echocardiography showed essentially normal mechanical valve function and LVEF 47%, and he met the criteria for discharge.
